Leonardo da Vinci. From 1452 to 1519, an Italian polymath of the High Renaissance whose genius spanned painting, sculpture, engineering, anatomy, and science. Born in the small town of Vinci near Florence, he became the quintessential renaissance man, creating some of history's most iconic artworks while maintaining thousands of pages of scientific observations and mechanical designs. His legacy defines the era's ideal of the artist-scientist and remains the touchstone for human creative potential.

Leonardo embodied the Renaissance belief that art and knowledge were inseparable. His insatiable curiosity drove him to dissect corpses, study plant growth, sketch flying machines, and engineer canal systems, all while creating paintings that revolutionized how light, shadow, and human psychology could be rendered. He finished relatively few works, yet each became a masterpiece that influenced centuries of artists. His notebooks, written in mirror script and filled with observations ahead of their time, reveal a mind that saw connections between all domains of knowledge.

Born in 1452 in the town of Vinci near Florence as the illegitimate son of a notary, Leonardo apprenticed under Andrea del Verrocchio, one of Florence's greatest sculptors and painters. He developed sfumato, a technique of layering transparent glazes and soft shadows to create luminous, atmospheric effects, a revolutionary departure from the sharp contours of earlier Renaissance art.

Leonardo painted the Mona Lisa, circa 1503 to 1519, an oil portrait of a Florentine merchant's wife with an enigmatic smile and unprecedented psychological depth, now the world's most famous painting. He created the Last Supper from 1495 to 1498 in the refectory of the Convent of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan, capturing the moment of Jesus's announcement of his betrayal with dramatic emotion and mathematical composition.

He produced the Vitruvian Man, circa 1490, a drawing of a nude male figure inscribed in both a circle and square, illustrating the ideal human proportions and the harmony between geometry and the body. Leonardo conducted detailed anatomical studies by dissecting cadavers, producing thousands of precise drawings of muscles, organs, and the circulatory system that anticipated modern anatomical science by centuries.

He filled notebooks with designs for flying machines, tanks, submarines, parachutes, and hydraulic pumps, engineering concepts so sophisticated that many would not be realized until centuries later. Leonardo served powerful patrons including the Medici family in Florence, Duke Ludovico Sforza in Milan, King Francis I of France, and the Borgias, allowing him to work across Italy and Europe. He moved between cities throughout his life, leaving works unfinished and ideas scattered across notebooks. By age 67, he had produced fewer than 20 paintings but each was a revolutionary masterpiece.
